prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength made optical time standards at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part, two-laureate prize, and round 1 has sharpened rather than changed my reasons. The test I apply is whether the achievement can be stated without leaning on the 2005 and 2012 prizes. It can: choose the trapping wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels for the clock transition, and thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated Doppler-free and recoil-free. The comb prize honoured the means of counting optical cycles, and the ion-trapping prize honoured control of single quantum systems. Neither honoured a many-atom clock whose main perturbation cancels by design. The original idea is Katori's, and the realisation at the accuracy frontier was driven by Ye's group, so the two roles are distinct and the pair is not a compromise. The result is verified many times over: Sr, Yb and Hg clocks agree in frequency ratios between laboratories on several continents, and fibre-linked comparisons are routine. It is a door-opening tool in the sense I care about, since millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and relativistic geodesy were not accessible before it. I would write the citation around the lattice and the magic wavelength, and not around timekeeping in general, so that it does not read as a lifetime or field award.
statement.case_against: The overlap with Hall and Hansch (2005) and Wineland and Haroche (2012) remains the objection that a careful reader will raise first, and Lindroth and Kroll are right that it depends on the citation wording. A broad wording would invite the charge of rewarding a more elegant successor to recognised work. The priority record is also not closed by anything in the round-1 exchange: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Hollberg lineage are outside the two names, and I have said the record should be checked in the primary literature, not argued from memory by AMO members among ourselves. Mehlig and Eriksson also raise a fair question, whether the committee is preferring mature precision measurement over a conceptual advance in understanding. I do not think the clocks fail that test, but I accept that they are a measurement achievement, and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether the committee is weighing mature precision metrology above a conceptual advance, warns against equating unanimity among the experimentalists with the strongest scientific case, and asks whether Ye's role is fairly described as implementation of Katori's idea.
responses.response: The warning against counting experimentalists is fair, and I am not treating the five-member alignment as evidence. On Ye I would say that the credit I propose is not 'implementation': Katori conceived magic-wavelength trapping and the first lattice demonstrations, while Ye's group took the lattice clock to the 10^-18 accuracy and stability frontier and developed the comparison and many-body work. These are two original contributions and the citation should say so by naming both invention and realisation. On B020 I agree with Eriksson's earlier point and your own candour that the hexatic evidence is system-dependent. As an experimentalist I would be asking what, precisely, was verified in nature, and I do not yet have a clean answer for a citation. Your willingness to accept B043 as a defensible outcome is noted, and I would keep B020 off my alternatives for that reason, though I do not dismiss the theory.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers twisted bilayer graphene as prediction confirmed by experiment, accepts that the pairing mechanism is open and that Yuan Cao is not among the credited names, and names optical lattice clocks as the fallback if recognition is judged premature.
responses.response: I take the prediction-then-confirmation structure seriously and keep B029 as my second alternative. But I cannot yet be 'absolutely sure' that we have identified the people who did the original experiment. The Cao omission is not a detail for me, since the 2018 papers rest on experimental work that the Jarillo-Herrero group credits to a first author we would be leaving out, and the community of Dean, Kim, Yacoby and others reproduced and extended it. I also note that the clocks have the same prediction-and-verification structure that you like: the magic-wavelength condition was proposed and then verified quantitatively. I agree with Pearce that the unresolved pairing mechanism is not by itself disqualifying. My hesitation is the combination of that open question, the very young record and the credit problem, which the clocks do not share. Your fallback remark is, I think, an honest statement of where the committee stands.

responses.point: Lindroth reads lattice clocks as a discovery about what a quantum system can be made to do, supplies the AMO priority record (the proposal is Katori's, the strontium implementation and record accuracy come from both groups), and asks whether Ye's scope makes the citation delicate.
responses.response: Her priority account matches the record as I understand it, and it is the best answer so far to the chair's question on the pair, though it is still from colleagues' knowledge and not from a primary-source review, which I would still want. I agree with her that the redefinition of the second is a consequence of the result and not a test of it. Where I differ slightly is on the word 'discovery': I would prefer 'invention and realisation', which is the committee's own language for an instrument-level contribution, and which answers the objection that no new phenomenon was found. I keep the citation narrow to the lattice clock, so Ye's comb and molecule work stays outside it.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B010) with Halzen and Karle as a discovery in the plainest sense, confirmed through several channels, and asks the committee not to let breadth of opening support replace the discovery character of the case.
responses.response: I share his regard for B010, ranked it second, and agree that the diffuse flux is the discovery and the source associations are the second chapter. I do not think breadth of support should decide the matter, and I do not rely on it. My difficulty remains the one I stated and which he states himself: Halzen and Karle against Halzen, Karle and Yoshida, and the AMANDA pioneers, and I cannot say that I am sure we have the right people. A prize with that open question is a prize I would rather not make this year. If the expert reports settle the roles, I would be glad to see B010 as a leading candidate next year, and I would not oppose it in a combined configuration, but the three-person cap means it cannot be paired with B043 without cutting a name, which I am not willing to do.

responses.point: Kroll asks for the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly, argues that the many-atom Doppler-free scheme is a distinct conceptual step from combs and ion clocks, and says the priority record on Lemonde and Takamoto should be checked.
responses.response: I agree on all three points and my citation follows his wording. I would add that the question of whether to wait for the redefinition of the second has, I think, been answered by Johansson and Pearce: it is a decision of a metrology body and not a scientific criterion, and the prize should stand on demonstrated reproducibility. On Takamoto, I note that he is credited with the first lattice-clock realisation together with Katori, which is the most serious concern for a two-name prize. I accept that the committee must decide whether that is a sufficient reason to widen the set, and I am not yet convinced it is, because the conceptual proposal and the accuracy programme are what the prize would recognise.

responses.point: Johansson moved B043 up after round 1, wants the citation to name the lattice and magic-wavelength concept explicitly, and disclosed that he should recuse on circuit QED and probably on B015 and B003.
responses.response: I welcome the move and agree on the explicit wording. I also note, for the record, that his recusal on circuit QED means that if the committee returns to B023, I would expect the discussion to proceed without him, and I do not see a conflict for B043 on either side. I concur with his reasoning that giving another superconducting-circuits prize one year after 2025 would invite the appearance of favouring one community, and that the four-name credit problem makes B023 the harder candidate this year.

uncertainties: Priority within the lattice-clock lineage: whether the primary literature supports Katori and Ye alone or requires Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow or others, which I cannot settle from memory and which needs an outside expert reviewer.
Whether the citation wording ('invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks') separates the achievement from the 2005 and 2012 prizes sufficiently in the eyes of the wider community.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second; I regard it as a confirming milestone and not a condition, but I cannot verify its timetable.
Whether IceCube credit among Halzen, Karle, Yoshida and the AMANDA pioneers can be settled, which decides whether B010 should be preferred in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B043. I have no known collaboration with Katori, Ye or their groups. I disclosed in round 1 that Goran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague; he has since reported that he would recuse on circuit QED, and I see no need for me to recuse on any shortlisted candidate. My own background is electron microscopy, so for the atomic-physics priority question I rely on colleagues and on expert reports.
